title: The stranger, the widow, the orphan (Exodus 22:21–27)
hook: you were strangers in Egypt; if he cries to me, I will hear

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second half of the ten words, lo tirtzach among them, ending with the one about wanting. Your line was ten words for living. Which one did you keep carefully? Day three hundred ninety-six.

It's your first week in a new country. You don't know which line to stand in. You can't read the forms. Someone at a counter speaks to you slowly and loudly, as if you were a child, and the people behind you sigh. You smile, because you need what's at the end of that line. A new school, a new job, a hospital in another city can give a small taste of it. Right after the ten words, Exodus starts filling in what they look like on the ground. And soon the law turns to exactly that person: the one who doesn't belong yet.
screen: `YOUR FIRST WEEK IN A NEW COUNTRY.` → `THE WRONG LINE, THE WRONG FORM.` → `THE LAW TURNS TO THAT PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger: someone living among a people who isn't one of them. Not a tourist. A neighbor without roots, without land, without family to stand up for him. And notice the reason. Not, because it's polite. Because you remember. You were the ones in the wrong line once. A chapter later the law says it again even more tenderly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Then the circle widens. "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." In the world of the text, a widow or an orphan could easily be left with no one to speak for them, and nothing to stop them being pushed aside. And here the text does something startling. God steps in personally. If you afflict them and they cry to me, he says, I will surely hear their cry. Then the law gets very small and very practical. If you lend to a poor neighbor, don't charge interest. If you take his cloak as a pledge, give it back before the sun goes down. Why? Because "that is his covering only," and the text asks, wherein shall he sleep? And God's reason: "when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious." Some Christians hear an echo in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." The stranger, the widow, the orphan: three people with no one else to stand up for them.
screen: `GER: SOMEONE WITHOUT ROOTS.` · `YOU KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.` · `THE WIDOW AND THE ORPHAN.` · `GIVE BACK THE CLOAK BY SUNDOWN.` · then, large: `FOR YE WERE STRANGERS IN THE LAND OF EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give to someone in need. Settle, and breathe. First remember a time you were the stranger: new, lost, unsure where to stand. Feel it again for a moment. Then think of someone who's there now. A new coworker. A family who just moved in. A person on the corner you pass every day. Someone grieving, or a kid without much of a home. Pick one person, and one small thing you could give: food, money, time, a name remembered. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
The stranger. In Hebrew, ger: someone living among you without land or family. The law protects him because Israel remembers being one.
Your line: you were strangers too. Today, give one real thing to someone who's new, alone or in need, and give it before the sun goes down. Day three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some churches run food pantries, refugee resettlement programs and ministries to widows and orphans, and some Christians cite Exodus 22 and Matthew 25 together when explaining why.

original.note: Hebrew: a stranger or resident foreigner, someone living among a people without land or kin there.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to visitors.
what it means: protect the people with no one to stand up for them, because you remember being them.
what a scholar hears: ger, the resident foreigner; the law protects him with a memory, not a rule: ye know the heart of a stranger.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'most of us have had a small taste of that feeling' (telling the listener), 'one of the first people the law turns to', 'the easiest people to push aside', and 'the three the Bible keeps returning to' (unsourced superlative/count) in voice and trapdoor; the Matthew 25 echo is now quoted exactly (KJV 25:35) and framed as 'some Christians hear'; the myth reveal now quotes 22:23 exactly; practice's prayer line changed so it no longer repeats day 391's.

Exodus 22:27 KJV in full: 'For that is his covering only, it is his raiment for his skin: wherein shall he sleep? and it shall come to pass, when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious.' The script quotes two fragments; confirm.
